implementation_notes: The standard library supplies the pool: sync.Pool.Get() returns an item - calling the New function when the pool is empty - and Put offers it back, and the implementation shards per-P with work-stealing plus a victim cache so concurrent goroutines rarely contend. Its documentation defines the contract to design against: any item may be removed from the pool automatically at any time without notification, and Get may ignore the pool entirely, so pooled values must be rebuildable temporaries (buffers, encoders) rather than things whose identity or liveness matters. For stateful resources (database connections, workers) the pool that owns them - database/sql's own pool, a worker pool - is the right answer instead of sync.Pool.
code_sketch:
var bufPool = sync.Pool{New: func() any { return new(bytes.Buffer) }}

b := bufPool.Get().(*bytes.Buffer)
defer func() { b.Reset(); bufPool.Put(b) }()   // reset before reuse
b.WriteString(payload)
pitfalls: Items can vanish at any garbage-collection cycle and Get() may ignore the pool: never use sync.Pool to keep a resource alive or to amortise anything that must not be recreated.
A Pool must not be copied after first use (it embeds noCopy), and it has no size bound, no fairness and no eviction - it grows under load and shrinks only through GC.

Put without Reset is the Go cesspool bug: the next borrower sees the previous payload, which can leak data between requests; and a Pool used as a free list inside one short-lived object does not amortise at all.
